economy.overview: Economy is the single biggest block of the Prelims paper here: 215 questions over 2011–2023 (19.3% of available questions), asked every year. UPSC tests it mainly through multi-statement items (115 of 215) built on precise definitions of banking, monetary and external-sector concepts, with Banking & RBI alone supplying 59 questions. Volume jumped in 2016–19 (21.2 per year vs 12.2 in 2011–15), driven by a wave of scheme and new-institution questions, and settled at 17.2 per year in 2020–23. Recent papers have moved toward financial instruments, inflation–exchange-rate–bond linkages and global groupings, and 2023 switched heavily to 'how many correct' and Statement I–II formats.
keyFindings: Banking & RBI is the backbone: 59 questions (27.4% of Economy), asked in all 13 years with 3–6 every year; monetary tools (Bank Rate, SLR, MSF, OMO) recur in 2011, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2020, 2021 and 2023.
UPSC repeats concepts almost verbatim: 'most inflationary way to finance a deficit' appeared as ECO-UPSC-2013-11 and again as ECO-UPSC-2021-05 with the same options.

Social Sector Schemes were a 2016–2018 phenomenon (14 of 21 questions: 5, 6 and 3), mostly skill and education schemes; after a lull they returned in 2023 as health missions (JSY, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, health-system structure).
Capital Markets & Financial Instruments is rising: 11 of its 18 questions came in 2020–23 (masala, convertible and inflation-indexed bonds, NFTs, beta, capital vs money markets).
Inflation resurged after the pandemic: 7 of its 13 questions came in 2021–22, testing links between inflation, bond yields, RBI forex action and NEER/REER rather than just definitions.
Fiscal Policy & Budget is falling: 4 questions in 2011, then never more than 2 a year; FRBM (2018, 2020) and Finance Commission criteria (2015, 2023) are what survives.
Format shift in 2023: 13 of 19 Economy questions used the new 'how many correct' (8) or Statement I–II (5) formats, which first appeared that year; 2016 and 2022 each had 15 multi-statement items.

International bodies are a reliable source of easy marks: report/facility-publisher matching (WEO 2014, GFSR 2016, Global Competitiveness Report 2019, Gold Tranche 2020, RFI/RCF 2022) recurs across the period.

recurringConcepts.note: Asked as the direction of effect — what a cut or hike in Bank Rate/Repo/MSF does to liquidity and lending.
Purpose of statutory reserves and how changing them alters bank lending and the money multiplier.
Definition of OMO and its use to change money supply or sterilise forex flows.
Which transactions change aggregate money supply and how liquidity ranks across deposits and currency.
Most inflationary way to finance a deficit (near-identical wording in 2013 and 2021) and ways to cut deficits.
What counts as FDI vs FII/portfolio and where it sits in the capital account.
Classifying items into current vs capital account and identifying forex reserve components.
Whether devaluation, remittances or capital flows improve the CAD or reduce currency-crisis risk.
Matching IMF instruments (SDR, Gold Tranche, RFI/RCF), committees and flagship reports.
Terminology and obligations under WTO (boxes, TFA, TRIMs, TRIPS-linked GI law).

recurringConcepts.concept: Financial inclusion institutions (Lead Bank, SHG, microfinance, PSL)
recurringConcepts.note: Aims of the Lead Bank Scheme/Service Area Approach, SHG-bank linkage, microfinance services and priority-sector coverage.
Roles of NPCI/UPI/RuPay, MDR and payment-data rules.

studyStrategy: Master money and banking first (NCERT Class 12 Macro + RBI functions): Bank Rate, Repo, MSF, CRR/SLR, OMO, money supply and multiplier — the highest-yield area every single year.
Prepare cause-and-effect tables (rate cut → liquidity, devaluation → exports/CAD, inflation → debtors/bond-holders, US Fed tightening → capital flight) because UPSC tests direction of effects.
Keep a one-line card for every institution and report: publisher (IMF, World Bank, WEF, IFPRI), chair, parent ministry (BBB, FSDC, MPC, NPCI, NITI missions).
Track financial instruments and new-age finance from Economic Survey/RBI and news: bonds (masala, convertible, IIBs, SGBs), P-notes, NFTs, CBDCs.

For schemes, focus on objective, target group and nodal ministry of flagship health, skill and inclusion schemes; revise the current year's Budget and Economic Survey for G20, trade and PLI-type questions.
Practise the 2023 'how many statements are correct' and Statement I–II formats, which leave no room for elimination — accuracy on each statement matters.

environment.overview: Environment contributed 213 questions across 2011–2023 (about 19% of the available paper) and appeared every year, with a steady 12–21 questions a year. Biodiversity & Conservation dominates with 88 questions (41%), centred on protected areas, wetlands, threatened species and wildlife law, and it holds 22 of the subject's 23 map-based questions. Climate Change (43) and Pollution (32) lean on named international initiatives, specific pollutants and emissions sources, while Ecology & Ecosystems (36) tests textbook ecology and, increasingly, animal behaviour and natural history. Over time the paper shifted from straightforward ecology and protected-area matching towards initiative/organisation questions (peaking 2016–19) and, in 2022–23, towards 'How many are correct' and natural-history questions that reward wide reading over elimination.
keyFindings: Biodiversity & Conservation is the backbone: 88 of 213 questions, asked in all 13 years, and 22 of the 23 map-based questions (protected areas, tiger reserves, wetlands) sit in this theme.

Protected-area questions are overwhelmingly location tests: which state (2014-16 Dampa/Gumti/Saramati, 2018-09 Pakhui), which river or basin (2013-15, 2014-09, 2020-13), which reserve contains which sanctuaries (2019-16 Agasthyamala) and where a species lives (2020-05 Kanha barasingha, 2020-11 musk deer).

The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the most repeated law: Schedule I (2015-02 dugong, 2017-09 tortoise), hunting prohibition (2017-10), Schedule VI plants (2020-06) and protection outside PAs (2022-18), plus Community Reserves in 2023-14.

Climate Change peaked in 2016–19 (20 questions) on 'who launched / what is' questions about named initiatives — INDCs (2016-06), Green Climate Fund (2015-09), CCAC (2017-07), GACSA (2018-10), Climate Neutral Now (2018-12), Climate Action Tracker (2022-14), EP100 (2022-15).

Pollution questions target specific, often novel, chemicals and their sources: brominated flame retardants (2014-02), microbeads (2019-02), benzene (2020-03), magnetite particles (2021-07), BPA (2021-08), triclosan (2021-09), mercury (2023-01) and HFC uses (2023-09).

A clear natural-history turn since 2021: rolling-up defence (2021-13), filter feeders (2021-14), fungus-farming ants (2022-11), honeybee waggle dance (2023-04), tool-using orangutan (2023-08), nocturnal fauna (2023-03), Indian squirrels (2023-06) and extremophile microbes (2023-07).

Format has hardened: 11 of the 2023 Environment questions use 'How many are correct' or Statement I–II formats (e.g. 2023-01, 2023-07, 2023-11, 2023-14), removing the option-elimination shortcut used in earlier multi-statement items.

Environmental Laws, Policies & Institutions is the only rising theme (1 question in 2011–15, 5 in 2016–19, 8 in 2020–23), covering EPA-1986 bodies such as CGWA (2020-09, 2022-17), Biodiversity Management Committees (2023-15) and the National Policy on Biofuels (2020-01).

recurringConcepts.note: Asks what a Schedule listing implies, which species cannot be hunted, and how protection applies inside vs outside protected areas.
Montreux Record, wetland–state/river matching, wetland functions and the 2010 Wetlands Rules.
Which areas are tiger reserves, their states, corridor importance, M-STrIPES and Critical Tiger Habitat area.
Distinguishes national parks, biosphere reserves, eco-sensitive zones and community reserves by what local people may do.

recurringConcepts.concept: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and bodies under it
recurringConcepts.note: Asks which body (GEAC, CGWA, AWBI) is constituted under which Act and what powers the EPA gives the Centre.
Habitat (Chambal), threats (dams, nets, agro-chemicals), legal status and national aquatic animal.
Identify decomposers/detritivores/producers or the correct food-chain sequence.
What adds or removes CO2, ocean phytoplankton as sink, blue carbon and candidate sequestration methods.
Definition question on plant growth under higher CO2; it appears twice in the 2018 data (likely a duplicate entry).
Who runs or founded GCF, BioCarbon Fund, FCPF, UN-REDD+ and the New York Declaration on Forests, and what they aim at.
Causes of the Antarctic ozone hole, CFC/HFC uses and the Montreal Protocol.
Which pollutants come from thermal plants, steel, copper smelting or furnace oil, and which cause acid rain.
Feedstocks permitted under the National Policy on Biofuels, biomass gasification, algae biofuels and sugar by-products (2020-01/2020-12 look like a duplicate entry).

studyStrategy: Make Biodiversity & Conservation the top priority: build a state-wise and river-wise map list of national parks, tiger reserves, biosphere reserves and Ramsar sites, with one flagship species each.

Read the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (schedules, hunting, community/conservation reserves), the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and the CAF Act, 2016 at the level of 'which body, which Act, what power'.

Keep a running register of international environmental bodies and initiatives — who launched/hosts each (UNEP, World Bank, UNFCCC, IUCN, EU) and its single core aim — since Climate Change and conservation-body questions are mostly of this type.

Cover textbook ecology thoroughly (NCERT Class 12 Biology ecology units, a standard environment text): food chains, nutrient cycles, succession, ecosystem services, biodiversity gradients and hotspot criteria.
Add natural-history reading on Indian fauna and flora (behaviour, diet, habitat, nocturnality, mammals vs non-mammals, fungi and useful plants), which has grown sharply in 2021–23.

Practise 'How many are correct' items: each statement must be judged independently, so revise pollutant–source pairs (coal, smelting, e-waste, plastics, HFCs) as exact facts rather than for elimination.

science_technology.overview: Science & Technology supplied 184 questions (16.5% of the available paper) and appeared in every year 2011–2023, steady at roughly 10–22 per year. UPSC tests it mostly through multi-statement items (113 of 184) that ask what a technology does or does not do, often triggered by a term 'in the news'. Space Technology (31) and Biotechnology & Genetics (30) dominate, while IT, Communication & Computing rose from 3 questions in 2011–15 to 12 in 2016–19 and 8 in 2020–23. Pure textbook Chemistry and Physics have declined, giving way to frontier topics such as CRISPR, blockchain, Web 3.0, quantum computing and green hydrogen.
keyFindings: Space Technology is the only theme asked in all 13 years with no gap (31 questions), mixing orbit basics (geostationary orbit 2011, PSLV/GSLV 2018) with frontier physics news (Higgs boson 2013, IceCube 2015, black-hole merger 2019).
Gravitational-wave detection is a true repeater: eLISA (2017), Einstein's GR predictions (2018), black-hole merger (2019) and the Evolved LISA description (2020) were asked in four straight years.

IT, Communication & Computing is the clearest riser: 3 questions in 2011–15 vs 12 in 2016–19 and 8 in 2020–23. 2022 alone asked about SaaS, NFTs, Web 3.0, qubits and open-source platforms (CoWIN, DigiLocker, DIKSHA).
GM crops recur across the whole period: Bt brinjal (2011, 2012), GM mustard (2018), transgenic techniques (2019) and Bollgard (2021). Gene editing/CRISPR-Cas9 followed in 2018, 2019 and 2020.

Many questions are pure term-decoding ('sometimes seen in the news'): Project Loon, GL-10, Denisovan, WannaCry/Petya, transcriptome, Wolbachia, aerial metagenomics, ACE2 and Qubit are each answered just by knowing what the term means.

Chemistry is fading (rated falling, 11 questions, none in 2022–23), while textbook Physics now appears through applied contexts such as pressure cookers, sodium vs LED street lights and light-years (all 2021).
2023 introduced the 'how many are correct' format to S&T (accelerometer, aquaculture biofilters, cosmic objects, green hydrogen), which removes elimination shortcuts.
Clean energy recurs as a policy-plus-science topic: solar PV vs thermal (2014), net metering (2016), solar manufacturing and tariffs (2018), solar pumps (2020) and green hydrogen (2023).

recurringConcepts.note: Asked as objectives, controversies or techniques behind Bt brinjal, Bollgard and GM mustard.
Asked as term-identification (Cas9 as 'molecular scissors') or which edits are now possible.
Asked through eLISA's purpose, black-hole mergers and Einstein's predictions.
Tests IRNSS orbits/coverage, GPS uses, solar-storm effects on GPS, and which countries own systems.
Lists of activities; candidates must spot which IRS/satellite data can measure.
Compares Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, NFC, Li-Fi and VLC on range, speed and medium.
Statement questions on decentralisation, data control and token properties.
DigiLocker, BHIM, Digital India aims, Aadhaar APIs and open-source platforms like CoWIN/DIKSHA.
PV vs solar thermal, net metering, India's solar manufacturing and pump types.
Heavy water, thorium vs uranium, ITER, and why some Indian reactors are under IAEA safeguards.
Vaccine availability and platforms (PCV, vector, mRNA, inactivated) and virus types.
Pronuclear transfer and maternal inheritance of mitochondrial diseases, asked in consecutive years.

studyStrategy: Prioritise Space, Biotech and IT (84 of 184 questions): learn ISRO missions and launch vehicles, GM/gene-editing tools, and digital technologies at a how-it-works level.
Keep a running glossary of S&T terms from one year of newspapers and PIB/ISRO/DBT releases. Many questions only test what a buzzword refers to.
Use NCERT class 6–10 science for Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Health. These items are application-based (water at 4°C, flame zones, B/T cells) and easy marks.

For multi-statement items, watch for extreme words ('only', 'first', 'all', 'cannot'). Many wrong statements, such as Astrosat or Mangalyaan 'only country' claims and blockchain being 'about cryptocurrency only', fail on overstatement.
Revise India-specific policy hooks: IAEA safeguards, NavIC, Digital India platforms, solar and green hydrogen missions, CERT-In rules, and GM crop approvals.
Practise the newer 'how many statements are correct' format, which UPSC used for four S&T questions in 2023.

indian_polity.overview: Indian Polity contributes 159 questions (about 14% of available questions) and appears in every year from 2011 to 2023. Its weight has risen steadily from 8.2 questions a year in 2011-15 to 16.2 a year in 2020-23, peaking at 23 questions in 2017. UPSC mixes article-level factual questions (Supreme Court, Parliament, President, Fifth Schedule) with a large block of abstract conceptual questions on constitutionalism, liberty, rights and parliamentary government. Multi-statement items dominate (82), and 2023 moved sharply to 'How many' and Statement I-II formats.
keyFindings: Concept-heavy questions have grown since 2017: 'constitutional government means limited government' appeared in 2014, 2020, 2021 and 2023 (POL-UPSC-2014-05, 2020-04, 2021-04, 2023-01).
Article 21 is the most tested single article - privacy (2018, 2021), right to marry (2019) and due process (2023).
The 'Welfare State' in DPSP was asked almost verbatim twice (2015, 2020), and DPSP non-justiciability twice (2017, 2020).
13 of 159 answers are 'Neither'/'None', clustered in Parliament, Elections and Judiciary questions - UPSC frequently tests popular misconceptions.
The 2023 paper had 12 of 15 polity questions in 'How many' or Statement I-II format, up from almost none earlier.
Tribal protection is a steady cluster: Fifth Schedule, PESA and FRA are tested across 2012-2023 in two themes (Scheduled Areas and Schedules).
Presidential election vote values returned in 2018 and 2023, with three President questions in 2023 alone.
Judiciary themes now extend to the justice system - legal aid, Bar Councils, prisons, custody and parole (2020-2023).

recurringConcepts.note: Asks which Article protects privacy, choice of spouse, or what due process means.
One-line definitional questions on what a constitution or constitutional government does.

recurringConcepts.concept: Welfare State & economic justice in DPSP
recurringConcepts.note: Asks which part embodies the welfare state, economic justice or limits on wealth concentration.
Statements test whether Part IV is enforceable or limits legislature/executive.
Asks the purpose and consequences of declaring Scheduled Areas.
Tests the specific powers PESA and FRA give to the Gram Sabha.
Asks its origin and whether laws in it escape judicial review.
Asks the defining feature of parliamentary or cabinet government.
Tests Rajya Sabha's powers over Money/Finance bills and which bills go to joint sitting.
Tests the electoral college and how MLA/MP vote values are calculated.
Checks the scope of judicial review and that basic structure is judge-made, not defined in the text.
Asks whether the AG can speak, sit on committees or vote in Parliament.

studyStrategy: Treat Polity as a high-priority, every-year subject: master Laxmikanth's core chapters on Fundamental Rights, DPSP, Parliament, Judiciary and the President first.
Read NCERT Class 11 'Indian Constitution at Work' and 'Political Theory' for the growing block of conceptual questions on liberty, rights, constitutionalism and parliamentary government.
Learn exact article wording for traps (executive power in the President, no-confidence not in the Constitution, Speaker rules), as many answers are 'Neither' or 'None'.
Cover tribal governance as a single unit: Fifth/Sixth Schedules, PESA, FRA and PVTGs.
Practise 'How many statements are correct' and Statement I-II questions, since the 2023 paper switched heavily to these formats.
Add a light layer of legal current affairs: landmark judgments (privacy, Aadhaar, NJAC) and statutes like RPA, Legal Services Authorities Act and Contempt of Courts Act.

geography.overview: UPSC tests Geography (148 questions, about 13% of the paper) mainly through location: 88 of 148 questions are map-based, led by Indian rivers, lakes and reservoirs (20) and world places in news (17). Indian Physiography & Drainage and Climatology are the two biggest themes, with conceptual physical geography (atmosphere, oceans, Earth's motions) forming the second pillar. Volume dipped sharply in 2016–19 (about 7 per year) before rebounding to 22 questions in 2023, the highest of any year. The recent rebound is driven by map questions on rivers, hills and conflict regions, framed increasingly as 'how many are correct'.
keyFindings: Map is king: 88 of 148 questions are map/location-based, and in 2023 16 of 22 Geography questions needed a map.
Indian rivers recur almost every year — Brahmaputra tributaries (2014, 2016, 2017), Godavari and Eastern Ghats rivers (2015, 2021), lakes linked to rivers (2023).
Places in News is rising: 7 of 12 Mapping questions came in 2022–2023, on African coups (Chad, Guinea, Mali, Sudan), famines (Somalia) and conflict regions (Nagorno-Karabakh, Kherson).
Countries around seas are a favourite: Mediterranean-bordering states asked in 2015, 2017 and 2019; land borders of Afghanistan (2022) and Ukraine (2023).
Monsoon predictors return regularly: La Nina/El Nino (2011), Indian Ocean Dipole (2017), Ocean Mean Temperature (2020).
Universe & Solar System has faded: 11 of 14 questions came in 2011–2015, only 3 since.
'How many are correct' format arrived in 2022 (3) and surged in 2023 (9), removing elimination shortcuts on map matches.
Mineral questions shifted from distribution (Kodarma mica, 2013) to legal classification and state powers (2018, 2019, 2020) and coastal atomic minerals (2022, 2023).

recurringConcepts.note: Tributaries and courses of NE rivers in multi-select format.
Which rivers join or rise where, and river-pilgrimage town pairs.
Type of lake or reservoir-state matching.
Matching hills/peaks to regions or ranges.
Which countries or rivers touch which sea.

recurringConcepts.concept: Land borders of countries in news
recurringConcepts.note: Count or pick neighbours of Afghanistan/Ukraine.
Match news regions/towns to countries or events.
Identify famine-hit countries or refugee camps.
Statements on ocean phenomena and their monsoon impact.
Locations of reefs in India and globally.
Reasoning on seasons and the 21 June sun.
Coal quality/imports, thermal plants and major/minor minerals.

studyStrategy: Make the atlas your primary text: trace every Indian river with tributaries, every hill range, lake and reservoir — this covers the largest theme and most map questions.
Use NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography for Climatology, Oceanography and Earth's motions; focus on 'why' explanations, as statements test causation.
Keep a running world map of places in news (conflicts, coups, famines, refugee camps) for the 12–18 months before the exam; the theme has surged since 2022.
Memorise country-sea and land-border lists for Mediterranean, Black Sea, Caspian, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.
Practise 'how many are correct' sets, since 2023 used this format for 9 Geography questions and partial knowledge no longer helps.
Revise mineral and energy topics with a policy lens: MMDR classifications, coal dependence, coastal atomic minerals.

modern_history.overview: UPSC tests Modern History mostly through direct identification and multi-statement questions on constitutional milestones, the national movement and colonial policy. Constitutional & Administrative Developments dominates (23 of 90 questions), followed by the Gandhian era and Early Nationalism. Over 2011–2023 the paper has moved away from mainstream Gandhian movements towards lesser-known personalities, journals and organisations. Question counts peaked at 14 in 2018 and fell to 4 and 3 in 2022 and 2023.
keyFindings: Modern History gives 90 questions in 2011–2023, with a peak of 14 in 2018 but only 4 in 2022 and 3 in 2023 — the lowest counts in the period.

Constitutional & Administrative Developments is the backbone: 23 questions, at least one every year, covering Charter Acts (2018, 2019, 2023), GoI Acts 1919/1935 and commissions like Simon, Butler and Cripps.
The Swadeshi Movement of 1905 is the single most-recycled idea, returning in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020 and 2023 from different angles (boycott, Surat split, Desher Katha, National Handloom Day).

Gandhian Era questions are falling: 16 in total, but none in 2022 or 2023 per stats, while Personalities, Press & Culture is rising with obscure items (Vital-Vidhvansak 2020, 'Songs from Prison' 2021, colonial archaeologists 2023).
UPSC increasingly tests lesser-known figures and bodies — Bhil Seva Mandal (2021), Rakhmabai case (2020), Vidyasagar and Bethune school (2021), INA officers (2021) — rather than headline events.
Format is mostly direct (50) or multi-statement (34); pairs (5) appear for founder/organisation matching. All tagged questions are static textbook history.
Colonial education and land revenue policy form a compact cluster (Wood's Dispatch and Charter 1813 in 2018, Ryotwari 2017, revenue terminology 2020).

recurringConcepts.note: Asked as its proposals (Dominion status, provincial opt-out) and as the trigger for Quit India.
The most repeated idea: origin of boycott, Surat split, Desher Katha, National Handloom Day link.
Asked via its trigger, 8 August resolution, character and chronology.
Home Charges, Naoroji/Dutt as critics, and economic effects of British rule.
Asked twice in three years as 'significance of the 1929 session'.
Aim of the Act and how Gandhi used the Home Rule Leagues.
Specific provisions: end of monopoly, education grant, Governor General of India.
Meaning of dyarchy and which subjects were reserved.
Headquarters and members.
Founder E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker in pairs or direct form.
Her roles, Theosophical Society, and the Home Rule League's later avatars.
Kheda's cause, Champaran's significance, BHU 1916 as first major appearance.

studyStrategy: Make Constitutional & Administrative Developments your first priority: tabulate every Act, Charter, commission and mission from 1773 to 1947 with 2–3 provisions each.
Study Swadeshi, Moderate-Extremist split and Drain theory in depth — they recur more than any other topic.
Build founder/organisation/journal tables for reformers, tribal and peasant movements, and second-rung personalities; these power the pairs and identification questions.
Use one standard text (Spectrum or Bipan Chandra's 'India's Struggle for Independence') plus NCERT Class 8 'Our Pasts III' and Class 12 'Themes in Indian History III' for lesser-known facts.
Revise chronology — UPSC asks sequencing questions (2017, 2018) and 'which happened earliest' items.
Given the 2022–2023 drop to 3–4 questions, do not over-invest; aim for solid coverage of high-yield themes rather than exhaustive trivia.

agriculture.overview: Agriculture accounts for 58 questions (about 5% of the paper), asked every year from 2011 to 2023, typically 3–6 questions a year with a spike of 12 in 2020. Early years (2011–2014) focused on crop geography — which crop suits which region or state — while from 2016 the emphasis moved to policy (MSP, procurement, e-NAM, schemes) and sustainable practices (zero tillage, conservation agriculture, SRI, fertigation, biochar). Questions are mostly multi-statement (36 of 58), testing whether a practice or policy is correctly described. Several items are cross-listed with Geography (orchids, mixed farming, Gujarat, watershed, Kinnaur, cotton).
keyFindings: 2020 was the peak year with 12 Agriculture questions (12.6% of that year's available questions), driven by MSP/pricing (3) and soil and farming practices (4).
Major Crops is the largest theme (12 Qs) but falling — 8 of its 12 came in 2011–2014.
Sustainable farming practices are the rising area: zero tillage (2020), conservation agriculture (2018), SRI (2022), biochar (2020), nitrogen-fixing plants (2022).
MSP mechanics recur: crops covered (2018, 2023), FRP approval (2015), FCI economic cost (2019), procurement limits (2020).
Edible oils are a repeated trade angle: imports exceed domestic production (2018), largest agri import by value (2019), palm oil uses (2021).
Sugarcane is asked from many angles: Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative (2014), FRP (2015), bud-chip settlings (2020), least water-efficient crop (2021).
Water-saving technology is a steady thread: drip irrigation (2016), water conservation practices (2017), fertigation (2020).

recurringConcepts.note: Which crops get MSP, who approves it and the limits of procurement.
India's import dependence and palm oil uses.
Planting methods, pricing and water efficiency.
Benefits of minimum tillage, residue retention and crop rotation.
Advantages of drip and fertigation, in multi-statement format.
Neem-coated urea, Soil Health Card aims, fertilizer pricing and raw materials.
Identify the state/region suited to a crop or matching pairs.
Pulse uses and seasons, legume intensification, nitrogen-fixing plants.
Classifying crops by season and Kharif area trends.
Effects of salinization and practices that raise or reduce it.
Seed replacement, seed villages and seed-saving techniques.
APMC, e-NAM and NPOP/APEDA roles.

studyStrategy: Prioritise policy mechanics — MSP/CACP/CCEA, FCI procurement, e-NAM, APMC — since pricing questions are rising and overlap with Economy.
Study sustainable practices conceptually (zero tillage, SRI, conservation agriculture, fertigation, biochar) and be able to judge each benefit claim in a multi-statement question.
Revise NCERT crop geography (Class X Agriculture, Class XII India) for crop-region and Kharif/rabi items; also covers Geography overlaps.
Track the Economic Survey agriculture chapter for trade data (edible oil imports, rice exports) and scheme updates (PMFBY, KCC, Soil Health Card).
Prepare sugarcane and oilseeds/palm oil as mini-dossiers covering cultivation, pricing, water and trade angles.

international_relations.overview: UPSC tests International Relations mainly through facts about international organisations and groupings — membership, headquarters, mandates and terms seen in the news. The subject barely appeared before 2016, peaked with 9 questions in 2016, and has since settled at 2–6 a year with gaps (none in 2021). Organisations & Groupings make up 24 of 35 questions; bilateral relations, West Asia and country profiles are marginal. Recent papers lean towards UN procedures and conventions (UNCLOS, UNGA observer status, Global Compact for Migration).
keyFindings: IR is a recent addition: only 2 questions in 2011–15 versus 23 in 2016–19 and 10 in 2020–23; no IR question appears in 2011–13, 2015 or 2021.
2016 is the peak year with 9 questions, most of them 'seen in the news' items on trade blocs and EU bodies (TPP, RCEP, BRI, European Stability Mechanism).

International Organisations & Groupings dominates with 24 of 35 questions; membership identification alone appears 6 times (Arctic Council 2014, GCC 2016, ASEAN FTA 2018, G20 2020, India's memberships and Turkic States 2022).
China-linked or BRICS development finance is a favourite: BRICS (2014), New Development Bank (2016) and AIIB (2019, 2022).
Since 2019 the focus has shifted to UN conventions and procedures — UNCAC/UNTOC (2019), UNCLOS (2022), UNGA observer status and Credentials Committee (2022), Global Compact for Migration (2023).
The split is almost even between static (18) and contemporary (16) questions: the body being asked is chosen from the news, but the answer rests on its basic facts.
Bilateral relations get little attention (4 questions, last in 2019), so mains-style India-X relations reading earns little in Prelims.

recurringConcepts.note: Pick which listed countries belong to a grouping, or which body India belongs to.
Founding history, HQ, membership size and India's shareholding.
One-liner: which country/bloc a news term belongs to.
European Stability Mechanism, Digital Single Market, India-EU BTIA.
OPCW, Nuclear Security Summits, NSG, MTCR, Hague Convention.
Credentials Committee, observer status, GCM adopted by UN members.
Multi-statement tests of treaty content — UNCAC/UNTOC, UNCLOS, GCM.
TPP, RCEP and ASEAN's free-trade partners.
APMCHUD and UN-Habitat asked together in 2017.
Two-state solution and Arab Peace Initiative.

studyStrategy: Prepare a membership grid for 15–20 major groupings (G20, BRICS, SCO, ASEAN, GCC, Quad, Arctic Council, NSG, MTCR, Turkic States) — this is the highest-yield IR task.
For every international body in the news, note HQ, founding year, membership size, India's status and one core mandate.
Revise UN basics: General Assembly committees and observer status, specialised agencies, and key conventions (UNCLOS, UNCAC, GCM).
Use monthly current-affairs compilations for 'seen in the news' terms, but always link them back to the underlying organisation.
Give bilateral relations and country profiles low priority for Prelims; one revision of major agreements (Chabahar, nuclear deals) is enough.

other_thin_data.overview: This is a small catch-all group of 12 questions spanning Sports & Awards, Art & Culture and Medieval History; the dataset barely covers these areas, so no firm trend can be drawn. Art & Culture and Medieval items appear only in 2014 and 2018 and test static facts such as temple styles, classical languages and philosophy schools. Sports & Awards (5 questions in 2021 and 2023) is the only recent cluster and is fully current-affairs driven.
